items.title: Snapdragons disprove Mendel's simplest law in one cross
items.claim: Red snapdragon crossed with white snapdragon. Mendel's dominance rule says: offspring should all be red (or all white). Snapdragon offspring are PINK. The textbook law fails on its very first test.

options.text: Mendel's laws don't apply to plants

Incomplete dominance — heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype because neither allele fully masks the other; the red allele encodes a pigment enzyme, and one functional copy produces only half as much pigment as two
Pink is a separate allele not from either parent

items.reveal:
Mendel happened to choose seven traits in peas that were all controlled by single genes with full dominance and complete penetrance. Most real traits are not.

Incomplete dominance: heterozygotes show intermediate phenotypes. Pink snapdragons. Pink camellias. Light pink human skin (one functional MC1R copy).

Codominance: both alleles fully expressed simultaneously. Human ABO blood group (a person with A and B alleles has both A and B antigens on red cells).

Epistasis: gene A's effect depends on gene B's genotype. Coat colour in Labradors (E gene controls whether B gene's brown/black is visible at all).

Polygenic inheritance: traits like height controlled by hundreds of small-effect genes. Family resemblance plus 'regression to the mean'.

Real genetics is much richer than 'dominant masks recessive'.
items.why: Mendel's laws are presented as universal. They describe a subset of inheritance patterns. Even simple breeding shows the laws don't always apply directly.

items.title: Each of your sperm/eggs is one of 2 to the 23rd power possibilities
items.claim: Meiosis shuffles 23 chromosome pairs into 23 gametes. From you alone, ignoring recombination, that's 8.4 million possible combinations. Add crossing over and the count is effectively infinite. Why is sexual reproduction so expensive to maintain?
items.prompt: Why has sex (rather than cloning) persisted in almost all eukaryotes?

options.text: Sex is uniformly better than cloning

Sex generates genetic variation that helps populations adapt to changing environments (the Red Queen hypothesis: ongoing host-parasite arms races favour variability); also recombination weeds out accumulated harmful mutations more efficiently than clonal lineages can
Sex is necessary for cell division

items.reveal_title: The twofold cost and the Red Queen
items.reveal:
A sexually reproducing female passes 50 percent of her genes to each offspring. An asexual female passes 100 percent. Asexual lineages should outcompete sexual ones by a factor of two each generation. They mostly don't.

Leading explanations:
- Red Queen (Hamilton, Van Valen): parasites and pathogens evolve to attack common host genotypes; sexual reproduction keeps host genotypes shifting so parasites can't catch up.
- Muller's ratchet: asexual lineages accumulate harmful mutations and cannot purge them efficiently. Recombination lets harmful mutations be separated from beneficial ones.
- Fisher-Muller: sex can combine beneficial mutations from different lineages.

Observationally, almost all asexual lineages are evolutionarily young, suggesting they accumulate problems and go extinct.
items.why: Sex's costs are enormous and obvious; its benefits are subtle and long-term. Evolution favours it anyway, and the reasons are still debated.

items.title: Your blood sugar is regulated within a 30% range despite irregular meals
items.claim: Normal fasting blood glucose: 4-6 mmol/L. After a meal: rises to 7-8, then back to baseline within 2 hours. Healthy people maintain this range whether they eat constantly or fast for a day.

options.text: Insulin (from pancreatic beta cells) lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and storage; glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it by mobilising stored glycogen — a classic antagonistic pair under negative feedback

items.reveal:
After a meal: blood glucose rises. Beta cells in the pancreas detect it via glucokinase and secrete insulin. Insulin tells muscle and fat to take up glucose, and the liver to store it as glycogen.

Between meals: glucose drops. Alpha cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon tells the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. If glycogen runs out (after ~24 hours fasting), gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol takes over.

Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of beta cells. No insulin. Blood glucose unregulated. Discovered to be treatable with injected insulin by Banting and Best (1921, Nobel 1923) — life expectancy of Type 1 patients went from months to decades within a year of insulin's availability.

Type 2 diabetes: insulin RESISTANCE develops in target tissues. Beta cells initially compensate (more insulin) then eventually fail. Affects ~10% of adults globally. Strongly linked to obesity and inactivity.

The brain is unique in burning glucose nearly exclusively (~120 g/day, 20% of total body glucose use) — which is why hypoglycaemia causes confusion, seizures and unconsciousness within minutes.
items.why: Hormones feel like signals from somewhere distant. In glucose regulation, two opposing hormones from the same gland keep blood sugar within a tight band — a textbook example of antagonistic negative feedback.
